subject: english-literature
title: Rhyme and Rhythm
welcome_lead: The music of poetry lives in patterns of sound and beat.
meta_desc: KS3 English Literature adventure on rhyme schemes, rhythm and meter.
final_note: You can now label common rhyme schemes and feel rhythm.

concepts.def: Same end sound on two or more words.
Regular pattern of beats per line.
Poetry with no fixed rhyme or meter.
Line or lines repeated through a poem.

walkthroughs.body_html: Use letters to map rhyme. AABB rhymes lines 1+2 and 3+4. ABAB alternates — common in ballads.
Rhythm is the felt beat; meter is the regular pattern. 'Da-DUM da-DUM' is iambic — Shakespeare's favourite.
Free verse has no fixed rhyme or meter. It still uses imagery and line breaks for effect.

mcqs.q: Lines rhyming as 1-2, 3-4 is which scheme?
options: AABB
ABAB
ABBA
Free verse

mcqs.q: Poetry with no fixed pattern is called.
options: Free verse
Sonnet
Haiku
Ballad

mcqs.q: Why must students distinguish the narrator from the author?
options: The narrator's views are always the author's views.
The narrator is a constructed voice within the text; the author is the real person who created it. Conflating them misreads irony, unreliable narration and persona.
The narrator and author are different words for the same thing.
Iambic pentameter is when every line rhymes.

mcqs.q: What are conventions of the Gothic genre?
options: Iambic pentameter is when every line rhymes.
Gothic refers to medieval architecture, not literature.
Settings of ruin and decay, supernatural or psychological terror, transgression of boundaries, the sublime, doubled or haunted protagonists, and atmospheric excess.
Gothic just means scary stories with vampires and ghosts.
Iambic pentameter is any line with ten syllables.
A line of five iambs (unstressed-stressed syllable pairs), creating a ten-syllable line with the rhythm da-DUM da-DUM da-DUM da-DUM da-DUM.
Iambic pentameter is when every line rhymes.
The narrator and author are different words for the same thing.
